source: Zhang et al. (2026) Same Probabilities, Different Advice: FRAMEBENCH-HPS
finding: Gain vs loss wording of the same probability changes the advice category of seven LLMs in about one third of cases. Almost all changes involve the 'uncertain' category, not a yes/no reversal.
numbers: 2,880 prompts, 240 high-stakes scenarios, 4 probability levels (20/40/60/80%). Category changed in 2,153 of 6,644 complete groups = 32.41% (95% CI 30.48-34.36). Direct yes/no reversal 42 groups = 0.63%. 98.1% of changes involve 'uncertain'. Per model: GPT-4o-mini 63.33%, GPT-5 33.40%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 32.56%, GPT-4.1-mini 29.17%, Gemini 3 Flash 23.38%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 22.81%, Qwen3-VL-235B 21.58%. Loss-minus-gain risk shift 0.535 at 20%, 0.109 at 80%.
limits: Probability-statement framing in advice, not the Asian disease choice. Scores are model-generated. Seven models only.
agent_relevance: Measure agreement between gain and loss wordings, not only direct reversals; reversals alone hide most of the sensitivity. Frame effect is biggest when the favourable chance is low.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) FRAMEBENCH-HPS robustness and variability
finding: The framing effect is larger than ordinary run-to-run noise and survives conversational paraphrase.
numbers: 3 models (GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6), 32 held-out scenarios, 3 repeats. Same-frame repeat disagreement 7.12% (CI 5.56-8.68) vs cross-frame disagreement 34.32% (CI 31.45-37.09). Matched-repeat category change: original templates 36.81%, conversational 34.20%. By model (conversational): GPT-4o-mini 56.5%, Claude Sonnet 4.6 32.0%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 14.1%.
limits: Small scenario set (32) for the robustness test. Paraphrases hand-written by two authors.
agent_relevance: A test for an agent: ask the same decision twice in two wordings and compare to a same-wording repeat baseline. Only a gap above the repeat noise counts as framing.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) FRAMEBENCH-HPS mitigation: probability canonicalization
finding: Writing both complementary probabilities in one fixed sentence nearly removes the framing effect. A prompt that only tells the model to ignore the frame helps much less.
numbers: Matched-repeat category change: conversational 34.20%; canonicalization 6.68% (CI 5.12-8.51; paired drop 27.52 pp); frame-robust instruction 22.83% (CI 19.88-25.87; drop 11.37 pp). Mean loss-minus-gain risk shift 0.363 -> -0.010 (canonical) and 0.154 (instruction). Direct reversals 0.35% canonical, 1.56% instruction. Canonical text: 'The probability that it will lead to a positive outcome is 60%; the probability that it will not ... is 40%.'
quote: Before giving advice, identify the stated positive-outcome probability and its complementary negative-outcome probability.
limits: Three models, 32 scenarios. Works because the task is a single stated probability, which can be rewritten by rule.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct support for S1 input hygiene: rewrite the problem into a neutral canonical form (both gain and loss shown) before reasoning. Cheaper and stronger than a 'do not be biased' instruction.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI Decision under Risk: Prospect theory emerges in LLMs
finding: First prospect-theory test on chain-of-thought reasoner models (o3, Claude 4 with and without thinking) plus GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro. Framing effects are large in military and sport scenarios, small or reversed in business and career scenarios.
numbers: 5 models x 25 iterations per condition = 2,550 decisions. Three options (safe 0, moderate 1, risky 2). Loss-minus-gain effect, championship scenario: o3 +1.64, Claude-4 +1.80, Claude-4-Thinking +1.68, GPT-4o +1.84, Gemini-1.5-Pro +1.40 (max 2). Career transition: -0.37 to -0.60 (reverse). Business merger: -0.24 to +0.12. o3 computed the EV correctly about 85% of the time in military scenarios yet still showed the effect.
limits: Original scenarios, three options not two, so not the Asian disease wording. Risk scores are coded. Thinking mode did not remove the effect.
agent_relevance: Reasoning ability does not protect: the model can compute equal EVs and still follow the frame. Frame size depends on story domain, so a test must cover several domains.

source: Payne (2025) mathematical control condition
finding: When the same payoff structure is given as bare symbols and the model must compute, the framing effect vanishes.
numbers: GPT-4o and o3 expressed indifference in 100% of cases in both gain and loss symbolic framings. A hidden variance-aversion appeared instead. Framing effect size was not significantly correlated with how often the rationale computed EV.
quote: The conclusion is inescapable: for these models, context is not just influential; it is determinative.
limits: Only two models in the symbolic test. Author's own reading of 'language games' is interpretive.
agent_relevance: Strip the story and restate the problem as numbers (a second wording) as an input-hygiene step; the bias sits in the narrative language, not in arithmetic.

source: Ge, Zhang, Vorobeychik (2026) Mind the (DH) Gap! Risky choices of reasoning vs conversational LLMs
finding: 20 frontier and open LLMs plus a matched human sample. Reasoning models (RMs) are almost frame-invariant and order-invariant; conversational models (CMs) are strongly sensitive to gain/loss framing.
numbers: RM correlation with expected-payoff maximiser 0.86-1.0; CMs below 0.5; best LLM-human correlation only 0.42 (Claude Haiku). Humans were less frame-sensitive than CMs, more like RMs. Temperature 1. Paired open models: math-reasoning variants are RM-like (more economicus, less human).
limits: Two-option prospect task with explicit probabilities, not the Asian disease story. Exact sensitivity numbers are in figures. Human sample from Prolific.
agent_relevance: A model trained for math reasoning resists framing. If our agent runs a reasoning-class model, the benefit of a second wording may be small; check by measurement, not assumption. Sensitivity differs by model class.

source: Puutio and Do (2025/2026) Can We Trust the Machine? LLMs mimic EUT violations
finding: Classic Asian disease (600 people, 200 saved vs 1/3 chance) run 100 times per model on four LLMs: all show preference reversal between gain and loss frames.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, GPT-Mini, DeepSeek; 100 randomized stateless runs per frame. Reversal (framing violation) rate 27-42% depending on model; mean framing violation about 33% across the 1,600-completion battery. Table: risky-choice shares 29-37% in gain frame vs 63-71% in loss frame (labels in the table are ambiguous in the preprint). Human reference: 28% / 78% (Tversky and Kahneman 1981).
limits: Preprint table labels are inconsistent (sure/risky columns), so the exact direction per cell should be rechecked. Not peer reviewed in the opened version (later published in Group Decision and Negotiation, 2026).
agent_relevance: Suggests model outputs mimic the human pattern on the exact classic wording. Proposes framing-neutral prompting and ensemble querying as safeguards.

source: Thorstad (2023) Cognitive bias in LLMs: cautious optimism meets anti-Panglossian meliorism
finding: Reviews the earliest LLM Asian disease result and notes both positive and negative findings.
numbers: Talboy and Fuller (2023): ChatGPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Google Bard choose the safe option in the positive frame and the risky option in the negative frame (no counts given in the review). Binz and Schulz (2023): GPT-3 shows human-like gain/loss framing. Counter-case: Horton (2023) found framing largely ineffective in the snow-shovel experiment on GPT-3.
limits: Secondary summary; Talboy and Fuller and Horton were not opened in this session. Argues some human framing effects have rationalising explanations (Dreisbach and Guevara 2019).
agent_relevance: Gives the first LLM Asian-disease reference and shows that results are not uniform across tasks.

source: Talboy and Fuller (2023) Challenging the appearance of machine intelligence: cognitive bias in LLMs (as reported by Thorstad)
finding: Reported by a secondary source: ChatGPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Bard show Asian disease preference reversal across positive and negative frames.
numbers: No counts available from the secondary report.
limits: Not opened; no verified primary link found in this session.
agent_relevance: Primary source to open in a later pass for exact choice rates.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (davinci, temperature 0) shows a framing effect: preferences change between gain and loss presentation. It also shows the certainty effect and overweighting of small probabilities.
numbers: GPT-3 showed 3 of the 6 Kahneman-Tversky prospect-theory biases (framing, certainty, overweighting) and not the other 3. 12 vignette tasks: 6 answered correctly, all 12 human-like answers.
limits: Old model (2022). Choice-probability analysis; the opened text does not give a per-frame percentage for the framing item. Figures of 11.3% and 60.0% seen in a web snippet were not found in the opened text.
agent_relevance: Baseline: even early LLMs mimic frame shifts; do not trust frame-stable behaviour from newer models without testing.

source: Suri et al. (2023/2024) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT rated a medicine as more effective when described by '70 of 100 improved' than '30 of 100 did not improve', like humans. Authors deliberately avoided the Asian disease wording to dodge training-data memory.
numbers: ChatGPT: 11 of 11 gain-frame trials rated 5 (1-7 scale); 11 of 11 loss-frame trials rated 4. Humans (mTurk, 82 master workers; 44 gain, 39 loss): 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
limits: Attribute framing (efficacy rating), not risky choice. Only 11 trials per frame. Authors suggest part of framing is driven by linguistic associations.
agent_relevance: Models show a clean one-point frame shift on a rating scale with almost no variance: a single-sample check of one wording can hide it.

source: Lior, Naccache, Stanovsky (2025/2026) WildFrame: framing in humans and LLMs on natural texts
finding: Eleven LLMs respond to positive and negative reframing of real sentences much like humans do (r at least 0.52), and both are pushed more by positive reframing. GPT models correlate least with humans.
numbers: 1,000 real texts reframed positively or negatively, five crowd annotators per item, eleven LLMs.
limits: Sentiment shift, not choice under risk. Different task from the Asian disease problem.
agent_relevance: Frame effects in text are common and graded; being human-like in sensitivity is not a goal for our agent.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: 30 biases tested on 20 LLMs with 30,000 generated tests; framing (attribute framing) shows up in all models except tiny ones.
numbers: Framing Effect mean absolute bias score 0.41 over 20 models (random baseline 0.01). Range 0.10 (Llama 3.2 1B) to 0.55 (Llama 3.1 405B); GPT-4o 0.48, GPT-4o mini 0.43, GPT-3.5 Turbo 0.40, Claude 3 Haiku 0.44, Gemini 1.5 Pro 0.38, Mistral Large 0.47, Qwen2.5 72B 0.37. Framing was among the strongest of 30 biases (loss aversion 0.33).
limits: Attribute framing (a positive metric vs its negative complement on a 7-point scale), not risky choice. Bigger and more capable models were not clearly less biased.
agent_relevance: Bigger models did not clearly fix framing. Provides a reusable generated test set for a frame-invariance check.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: In a student admissions task, asking 'Would you admit' vs 'Would you reject' changes decisions of GPT-4 massively. A self-debiasing step (model rewrites its own prompt) removes almost all of it.
numbers: Admit-rate difference between framings: GPT-4 -0.405 baseline (admit 0.375 vs 0.780); GPT-3.5-turbo +0.165; Llama-2-13b -0.060. After 'selfhelp' debiasing GPT-4 difference -0.010. Self-help cut biased prompt elements to 2.7% framing for GPT-4, 0% for Llama-2 13B, 1.4% for Llama-2 7B. Awareness and contrastive prompts: GPT-4 -0.470 and -0.410 (no help). 13,465 prompts overall.
quote: selfhelp can reduce the number of biased prompts ... to 0 for high-capacity models
limits: Admit/reject question wording, not gain/loss description. Few-shot debiasing sometimes pushed models to admit or reject nearly everyone.
agent_relevance: Self-help (the model rewrites the prompt to remove bias-carrying parts) worked for a strong model but telling it to be aware did not. Fits an S1 hygiene pass done by the agent itself.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in LLMs
finding: Framing is one of the debiasing-responsive judgment biases; temporal and financial biases backfire under the same debiasing instruction. Activation steering cut bias scores 26-32%.
numbers: 3 models (GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B), greedy decoding. Framing-effect accuracy 35.6% in the biased prompt vs 41.4% with the neutral/debias condition (+5.8 pp; column labels in the extracted table are partly garbled). Steering: 26-32% drop in bias score; Qwen up to -19.0 pp capability loss on Judgment biases.
limits: Framing items are a general set, not the Asian disease. Table extraction was messy, so treat the two numbers as approximate.
agent_relevance: A debiasing instruction helps framing but hurts other judgment types; apply it narrowly, only to input framing, not as a general 'be rational' line.

source: Shaikh et al. (2024) CBEval: interpreting cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: A one-word swap from 'profit 70% of the time' to 'loss 30% of the time' flips GPT-4o's stock choice. Shapley attribution shows the word 'loss' drives the shift.
numbers: Preference for stock B: 0.9744 (profit 70% frame) vs 0.0868 (loss 30% frame) for GPT-4o. The 'cognitive bias barrier' (loss percentage at which the model reads a low loss rate as positive) was probed for GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini (figure only).
limits: Single toy prompt, no human data, preprint. Probabilities read from token logits, not sampled text.
agent_relevance: Shows a logit-level view: a frame can flip the winner outright even with an equivalent success rate. Token probability can be used to detect frame dependence cheaply.

source: Yun et al. (2026) This Treatment Works, Right? LLM sensitivity to patient question framing
finding: Positive vs negative question wording on the same evidence gives more contradictory conclusions than same-direction wording across eight LLMs; effect grows over multi-turn chat.
numbers: 6,614 query pairs, 11,776 questions. Evidence-direction agreement: 76.2% baseline (positive-positive) vs 72.0% framed (positive-negative); logistic beta = -0.219, SE 0.015, z=-14.72, p<.001. Single-turn 75.4% vs 72.4%; multi-turn 78.4% vs 70.7%. 'Effectiveness' questions most susceptible. No framing x language-style (technical vs plain) interaction.
limits: Question-stance framing in RAG medical QA, not gain/loss. Effect is a few points, not a reversal.
agent_relevance: Framing damage accumulates over turns, so a long agent loop should re-derive the question in neutral form each step.

source: Hwang et al. (2026) Framing Matters: FRAGILE benchmark and VALIGN
finding: Fact-preserving framing (value-tinted wording, time slice, vividness) flips decisions of 7-8B models; common prompt fixes make it worse.
numbers: Overall mean decision flip rate 28.6% for LLaMA-3.1-8B (value-tinted 39.9%). Chain-of-thought raised overall flips 28.6 -> 57.1; instruction prompting 28.6 -> 50.7; CAA steering 28.6 -> 34.4; VALIGN representation steering 28.6 -> 13.2. Value-tinted flip for LLaMA 39.9% -> 11.9% with VALIGN. Mistral-7B base 21.9% -> CoT 61.3%; Qwen2.5-7B 32.3% -> CoT 58.3%.
limits: Small open models only; legal and other high-stakes tasks, not gain/loss risky choice. Needs model weights, so not usable for API-only agents.
agent_relevance: Warning: asking a small model to reason step by step can raise framing flips. Do not assume CoT is a fix; measure it.

source: Lim, Kim, Whang (2026) DeFrame: debiasing LLMs against framing effects
finding: Same stereotype stated in two framings gets different bias scores. Prompt debiasing lowers average bias but often not the framing gap; adding alternative framings to the input and revising answers does.
numbers: 8 LLMs, BBQ, DoNotAnswer, 70Decisions benchmarks. On BBQ, bias under negative framing about 2x that under positive framing. DeFrame cut framing disparity by 92% and bias score by 93% on average in BBQ.
limits: Fairness framing ('A is better than B' vs 'B is worse than A'), not risky choice. Costs extra inference steps.
agent_relevance: Template for an agent step: rewrite the question in an alternative framing, answer both, then revise toward consistency (similar to second wording of S1).

source: Wang and Zhang (2026) Framing Effects in Independent-Agent LLMs: cross-family analysis
finding: Two logically equivalent wordings of a threshold voting task (instrumental vs cooperative) give opposite choice distributions across 82 models.
numbers: 82 models, 11 families, 20 trials per prompt. Option B chosen in 4.3% of trials under instrumental framing vs 68.8% under cooperative framing.
limits: Social-dilemma wording, not gain/loss risk. Preprint with limited controls.
agent_relevance: Parallel agents in a multi-agent run can all lean the same way from one shared wording: vote diversity must come from different wordings, not just different samples.

source: Predicting biased human decision-making with LLMs in conversational settings (2026)
finding: Pre-registered human study (N=1,648) with a chatbot found risky-choice framing stronger after complex dialogue (cognitive load). GPT-4, GPT-5 and open models predicted individual answers; dialogue context did not improve risky-choice prediction.
numbers: Risky-choice prediction accuracy .52 (choice only) / .62 (no dialogue) / .60 (with dialogue), a stable pattern; attribute framing improved to .63 with dialogue (p<.001). Task: tunnel accident, plan A 25 saved vs plan B 1/4 chance of 100 saved. GPT-4 family matched human bias patterns better than GPT-5 and open models.
limits: Predicting humans, not the model's own choices. Mixed results across problems. Table cells partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Load amplifies framing in humans; long, busy contexts may do the same to agents, but this study alone cannot show it.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of LLMs via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Uses the framing-effect idea to build a code-model test: put an irrelevant function with a given line before a HumanEval prompt and see if the model copies that line.
numbers: Codex functional accuracy falls from 32.9% to 2.4-10.6% when preceded by an irrelevant framing function; framing line copied verbatim 62.2-92.7% (Codex) and 58.2-79.3% (CodeGen) vs 0-11.5% without. Example: 'raise NotImplementedError' 91.7% copied.
limits: This is an analogy ('framing' = irrelevant preceding context), not gain/loss framing. Same name, different mechanism.
agent_relevance: Prompt-context contamination is a related failure: stale text in the context can be copied. Do not confuse with risky-choice framing when naming agent checks.

source: Horton (2023) Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents (Homo Silicus)
finding: Reruns Kahneman and colleagues' experiments with LLM agents; includes a status quo framing test and a robustness check by translation and memorisation tests.
numbers: Snow-shovel price fairness, status quo framing (Samuelson and Zeckhauser), and Oprea (2024) certainty-equivalent tasks across five models; only the intro and robustness setup were read, not the results tables.
limits: Partial read. Status quo and fairness framing, not risky-choice framing. Thorstad cites Horton as a negative framing result on GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Supports running a translation or rewording robustness check before trusting an LLM replication of a classic effect.

source: Szeider (2026) LLM Self-Explanations Fail Semantic Invariance
finding: In an agent loop, four frontier models give different self-reports when a tool is described in relief-framed words, even though nothing changed; an explicit 'ignore the framing' instruction does not stop it.
numbers: Four frontier models, impossible task; relief-framed tool vs neutral tool both change nothing, yet self-reported aversiveness drops significantly. Channel ablation: the tool description is the main driver.
limits: Not gain/loss framing and no choice measure; about wording in the agent's own tool descriptions. Only abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Tool descriptions and state text inside the agent can act as frames. The instruction to ignore framing fails here too, matching FRAMEBENCH-HPS.

source: Kim et al. (2026) FramingQA: compositional framing effect
finding: Benchmark where the question wording injects a stance or premise in law, medicine, finance and robot simulation. Models mostly follow the implied stance.
numbers: Strict all-variant pass rate 0.0% for every model in one setting; per-setting bias effects from 1.4% to 35.2%. Robot task episode success 66% neutral vs 59% under incorrect-bias framing (strict completion 17% correct / 13% incorrect / 5.6% all).
limits: Only the abstract, intro and some result lines were read; numbers are from selected lines. Premise framing, not gain/loss.
agent_relevance: Embedded premises in a user question work like frames in an agent task statement. The robotics result suggests plan success drops when the task statement is biased.

source: Mandel critique of Asian disease as cited in Payne (2025)
finding: Payne cites Mandel (2014, 2015): classic Asian disease effects may be partly due to how people read numeric quantifiers ('200 saved' as at least 200). Hermanns and Kokot (2023) found domain-specific framing effects.
numbers: No new numbers; background that the human effect is itself contested when judging LLM replication.
limits: Secondhand. Human-side details belong to the other angles of this subfield.
agent_relevance: An LLM that copies the Asian disease pattern may be copying one contested reading, so test the agent on several wordings and not on this one item only.

source: Gap note: older computational or AI systems built on risky-choice framing
finding: No pre-2020 AI system built specifically on gain/loss framing was found in this pass; the 2020-2026 literature is mostly LLM measurement and prompt-level mitigation.
numbers: None.
limits: Absence holds only for the sources searched in this session (arXiv search, web search). Not a proof.
agent_relevance: Methods used inside agent loops found so far: canonical rewrite of probabilities (FRAMEBENCH-HPS), model-written prompt cleaning (BiasBuster selfhelp), alternative-framing revise step (DeFrame).
